The worst a prince can expect from a hostile people is to be abandoned by them. From hostile nobles he must fear not only abandonment but attack; for the nobles see further and move earlier, they always act in time to save themselves, and they court favor with whichever side they expect to win. And besides, the prince has to live with the same people always, but he can do perfectly well without the same nobles, since he can make them and unmake them every day, and give or take away their standing as he pleases.

To make this part clearer, I say the nobles should be considered in two main ways: either they run their course so as to bind themselves entirely to your fortune, or they do not. Those who bind themselves, and are not greedy, should be honored and loved. Those who do not bind themselves come in two kinds. If they hold back out of faint-heartedness — a natural shortage of spine — then make use of them, especially the ones with good counsel in them; in prosperity they do you honor, and in adversity you have nothing to fear from them. But when they keep clear of you deliberately, for reasons of ambition, it is a sign they are thinking more of themselves than of you; and against those a prince must guard himself, and fear them as if they were declared enemies, because in adversity they will always help bring him down.

Therefore, one who becomes prince by the favor of the people must keep the people his friend — which is easy, since all they ask is not to be oppressed. But one who becomes prince against the people, by the favor of the nobles, must before anything else try to win the people over — also easy, once he takes them under his protection. And because men, when they receive good from someone they expected only harm from, bind themselves all the more tightly to their benefactor, the people become better disposed toward him at once than if he had been raised by their own favor. A prince can win them in many ways, but the ways vary so much with circumstance that no fixed rule can be given, and I will leave them out. I will conclude only this: a prince must have the people friendly — otherwise, in adversity, he has no remedy.

Nabis, Prince of the Spartans, withstood the siege of all Greece and of a triumphant Roman army, and against them defended his country and his own rule; and when the danger came, all he needed was to secure himself against a few — which would not have been enough if the people had been his enemy. And let no one counter this opinion of mine with the worn proverb that 'he who builds on the people builds on mud.' That is true when a private citizen lays his foundation there and lets himself believe the people will rescue him when his enemies or the magistrates come for him; in that case a man will often find himself deceived, as the Gracchi were in Rome and Messer Giorgio Scali was in Florence. But if it is a prince who builds on the people — one who can command, a man of spirit, unshaken in adversity, who does not neglect his other preparations, and who keeps the whole city's nerve up by his own courage and his own orders — he will never find himself betrayed by them, and he will find he has built on solid ground.

These principalities usually come into danger at the moment they are climbing from the civil order to the absolute one. For these princes rule either in their own person or through magistrates. In the second case their position is weaker and more dangerous, because it rests entirely on the will of the citizens who hold the magistracies — and they, especially in hard times, can take the state from him with great ease, either by moving against him or simply by not obeying. And in the middle of the danger there is no time for the prince to seize absolute authority: citizens and subjects who are used to taking their orders from the magistrates are not about to obey his in that crisis, and in uncertain times he will always be short of men he can trust. A prince like this cannot build on what he sees in quiet times, when the citizens need the state — then everyone runs to him, everyone promises, and with death nowhere in sight, everyone is ready to die for him. But in hard times, when the state needs its citizens, few are to be found. And this experiment is all the more dangerous because it can only be run once. So a wise prince must think of a way to make his citizens need the state and need him — always, in every kind of weather. Then they will always be faithful.
books.title: The Civil Principality

books.label: Chapter X
paragraphs: In examining the qualities of these principalities, there is one more question to consider: whether a prince has a state strong enough to stand on its own at need, or whether he will always need someone else's protection. To make the point clearer, I say that in my judgment those princes can stand on their own who have enough men or enough money to put together a proper army and meet in the field whoever comes to attack them; and those always need others who cannot take the field against the enemy, but are forced to fall back behind their walls and defend them. The first case has been discussed, and later I will say whatever more it needs. In the second case there is nothing to say except to urge such princes to fortify and provision their own town, and to take no account of the countryside. Whoever has fortified his town well, and has handled his subjects in the way described above and to be described again, will never be attacked except with great hesitation; for men are always wary of ventures where the difficulty is plain to see, and no one sees an easy target in a prince whose town is strong and whose people do not hate him.

The cities of Germany are completely free, they have little surrounding territory, and they obey the emperor when they choose to; they fear neither him nor any other power near them, because they are fortified in such a way that everyone reckons taking them would be slow, grinding work. They all have proper moats and walls; they have artillery enough; they keep enough in the public stores to eat, drink, and burn for a year. Beyond that — to keep the common people fed without cost to the public — they always hold in common a year's worth of work to give out in the trades that are the nerve and life of the city, the industries the people live by. They keep military exercises in good repute, and have many ordinances besides to maintain them.

So a prince who has a strong city and does not make himself hated cannot be attacked; and even if someone did attack him, the attacker would leave in disgrace — because the affairs of this world are so changeable that it is next to impossible to sit idle with an army for a whole year while you besiege him. And to whoever answers that if the people have their property outside the walls and watch it burn, they will lose patience, and the long siege and their own self-interest will make them forget the prince — I reply that a powerful and spirited prince will always get past those difficulties: now giving his subjects hope that the evil will not last long, now stoking fear of the enemy's cruelty, now deftly securing himself against the ones who seem too bold.

Besides, the enemy will naturally burn and wreck the countryside on arrival, while the defenders' blood is still hot and willing; so the prince has all the less reason to worry, because after a few days, when tempers have cooled, the damage is already done, the losses already taken, and there is no undoing them. And then the people close ranks with their prince all the more, feeling he is now obliged to them, their houses burned and their lands ruined in his defense. For it is the nature of men to be bound by the benefits they give as much as by the benefits they receive. So all things considered, it will not be hard for a prudent prince to keep his citizens' minds firm through a siege, from first day to last — so long as they lack neither food nor the means to fight.
books.title: Measuring a State's Strength

books.label: Chapter XI
paragraphs: It remains now only to speak of ecclesiastical principalities. With these, every difficulty comes before you possess them: they are acquired by virtù or by fortune, and kept without either, because they are sustained by the ancient institutions of religion, which have grown so powerful, and are of such a kind, that they keep their princes in power however those princes act and live. These princes alone have states and do not defend them, subjects and do not govern them; and the states, though undefended, are not taken from them, and the subjects, though ungoverned, do not care — they neither think of breaking away, nor could they. Only these principalities, then, are secure and happy. But since they are upheld by a higher cause, which the human mind cannot reach, I will say no more about them; they are raised up and maintained by God, and it would be the work of a presumptuous and reckless man to pass judgment on them.

Still, someone might ask me how it happens that the Church has risen to such greatness in temporal power — given that until Alexander the Italian powers, and not only the ones called powers but every baron and lord down to the smallest, held that temporal power cheap, and now a king of France trembles before it, and it has been able to throw him out of Italy and to ruin the Venetians. Well known as this is, I do not think it wasted effort to call some part of it back to mind.

Before Charles, King of France, came down into Italy, this country was under the rule of the Pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the Florentines. These powers had two chief anxieties: that no foreigner should enter Italy in arms, and that none of their own number should seize more territory. The two watched most closely were the Pope and the Venetians. To hold back the Venetians it took a league of all the rest, as in the defense of Ferrara; and to hold down the Pope they used the barons of Rome. Divided into two factions, Orsini and Colonnesi, the barons never lacked a pretext for disorder; standing with weapons in hand under the Pontiff's own eyes, they kept the papacy weak and sickly. Now and then a spirited pope arose — a Sixtus — but neither fortune nor wisdom could ever rid him of this nuisance. The shortness of papal lives was the cause. In the ten years an average pope reigns, he could barely beat down one of the factions; and if one pope, so to speak, had all but wiped out the Colonnesi, up came a successor who was enemy to the Orsini — which raised the Colonnesi again — and there was no time left to wipe out the Orsini. This is why the Pope's temporal powers were held in little esteem in Italy.

Then came Alexander the Sixth, who showed better than any pontiff who ever lived what a pope with money and arms could do. Using Duke Valentino as his instrument and the French invasion as his occasion, he brought about everything I described above in discussing the duke's actions. His intention was to make the duke great, not the Church; but what he did made the Church great anyway, and after his death, and the duke's ruin, the Church inherited his labors.

Then came Pope Julius, and he found the Church strong: mistress of all the Romagna, the barons of Rome crushed, the factions beaten flat under Alexander's blows — and the road open to piling up money by methods never used before Alexander's time. Julius not only continued all this but improved on it. He set out to take Bologna, to snuff out the Venetians, and to drive the French from Italy; and every one of these enterprises succeeded, with the more credit to him because he did it all to strengthen the Church and no private man. He also kept the Orsini and Colonnesi factions within the bounds in which he found them; and though there were heads among them itching to make trouble, two things held them still: the greatness of the Church, which cowed them, and the fact that they were allowed no cardinals of their own — the origin of all their disorders. These factions will never be quiet while they have cardinals, because cardinals feed the factions, in Rome and beyond, and the barons are forced to defend them: from the ambitions of prelates come the discords and tumults of the barons. So His Holiness Pope Leo has found the papacy at the height of its power; and if others made it great with arms, one may hope that he, by his goodness and his infinite other virtues, will make it greater still, and revered.
books.title: Ecclesiastical Principalities

books.label: Chapter XII
paragraphs: Having discussed one by one the kinds of principality I proposed at the outset, having considered in some measure why they do well or badly, and having shown the methods by which so many men have tried to win and hold them, it remains for me now to speak generally of the offense and defense that each of them may require.

I said above that a prince must have solid foundations under him, or he necessarily comes to ruin. The principal foundations of all states — new, old, or mixed — are good laws and good arms. And since there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms, and where there are good arms there are bound to be good laws, I will leave the laws aside and speak of arms.

I say, then, that the arms with which a prince defends his state are either his own, or they are mercenary, auxiliary, or mixed. Mercenaries and auxiliaries are useless and dangerous. If a man rests his state on mercenary arms, he will never stand firm or safe; for they are disunited, ambitious, undisciplined, disloyal — swaggering among friends, cowardly before the enemy; no fear of God, no faith with men. Your ruin is put off only as long as the assault is put off: in peace you are stripped by them, in war by the enemy. The reason is that they have no love for you, and no cause to keep them in the field beyond a little pay — which is not enough to make them want to die for you. They are delighted to be your soldiers while you are not making war; when war comes, they desert or run. It should cost me little effort to prove this, since the ruin of Italy has been caused by nothing else than her resting all her hopes, for so many years, on mercenary arms. They did once make headway for certain men, and they looked brave enough against one another; but when the foreigner came, they showed what they were. So it was that Charles, King of France, was allowed to take Italy with a piece of chalk; and the man who said our sins were the cause of it told the truth — only they were not the sins he meant, but the ones I have described. And since they were the sins of princes, it is the princes who have paid the penalty.

I want to show the wretchedness of these arms more fully. Mercenary captains are either excellent soldiers or they are not. If they are, you cannot trust them: they will always be working toward greatness of their own, either by crushing you, their master, or by crushing others against your intent. And if the captain is no good, he ruins you in the ordinary way — by losing.

If the answer is that anyone with arms in hand will act this way, mercenary or not, I reply: arms are wielded either by a prince or by a republic. The prince should go in person, and do the captain's job himself. The republic must send its own citizens; when it sends a man who proves worthless, it must replace him, and when it sends a good one, it must bind him with laws so that he does not overstep the mark. Experience shows princes acting alone, and republics armed with their own arms, making enormous progress, and mercenary arms doing nothing but damage. And a republic armed with its own arms is far harder to bring under the rule of one of its citizens than a republic armed with foreign arms. Rome and Sparta stood armed and free for centuries. The Swiss are the best-armed people alive, and the freest.

As for ancient examples of mercenaries, there are the Carthaginians, who at the end of the first war with Rome were nearly crushed by their own mercenary soldiers, though the Carthaginians had their own citizens for captains. After the death of Epaminondas, the Thebans made Philip of Macedon captain of their forces; and after he had won, he took away their liberty.

When Duke Filippo died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza against the Venetians. He beat the enemy at Caravaggio — and then joined with the enemy to crush the Milanese, his employers. Sforza his father, in the pay of Queen Johanna of Naples, abandoned her defenseless in a stroke, so that to save her kingdom she had to throw herself into the arms of the King of Aragon. And if the Venetians and the Florentines did once enlarge their dominions with such arms, and their captains did not make themselves princes but defended them, I answer that in this the Florentines were favored by chance. Of the able captains they had cause to fear, some did not win, some met opposition, and some turned their ambition elsewhere. The one who did not win was Giovanni Acuto; and since he did not win, his loyalty was never put to the proof — but everyone will grant that had he won, the Florentines stood at his discretion. Sforza always had the Bracceschi against him, and each kept watch on the other; Francesco turned his ambition on Lombardy, Braccio against the Church and the kingdom of Naples. But come to what happened only yesterday. The Florentines made Pagolo Vitelli their captain, a very shrewd man who from private life had risen to great renown. If he had taken Pisa, no one can deny that the Florentines would have been bound to him: had he gone over to their enemies, they had no defense, and so long as they kept him, they had to obey him. As for the Venetians, look at their record, and you will see that they acted safely and gloriously so long as they made war with their own men — this was before they turned to enterprises on land — when gentlemen and armed commoners together fought with the greatest virtù. The moment they began to fight on land, they abandoned this virtù and took up the customs of Italy. In the early days of their expansion on land, having little territory there and a great reputation, they had little to fear from their captains; but as they expanded — under Carmignuola — they got a taste of the mistake. They had seen how supremely able he was; under his command they had beaten the Duke of Milan. But they also saw how cold he had grown toward the war, and they judged that with him they could win no longer, because he had no wish to win; yet they could not dismiss him, or they would lose again what they had gained. So, to secure themselves against him, they were forced to murder him. Since then they have had for captains Bartolomeo da Bergamo, Roberto da San Severino, the count of Pitigliano, and the like — men under whom the fear was of loss, not the hope of gain; as happened later at Vaila, where in one day's battle they lost what eight hundred years of hard labor had won them. From these arms come conquests that are slow, late, and feeble; and losses that are sudden and astonishing.

And since these examples have brought me to Italy, ruled now for many years by mercenary arms, I want to trace them from further back, so that once their origin and course are in view they can be better corrected. You must understand, then, how in recent times, as soon as the Empire began to be pushed out of Italy and the Pope gained more standing in temporal affairs, Italy broke up into more states. Many of the great cities took up arms against their nobles, who, favored by the emperor, had held them down, while the Church favored the cities to build its temporal power; and in many other cities, citizens rose to be princes. So Italy fell largely into the hands of the Church and of certain republics; and the Church being priests and the republics being citizens unaccustomed to arms, both began to hire foreigners.

The first to give this soldiery a reputation was Alberigo da Conio, of the Romagna. From his school came, among others, Braccio and Sforza, who in their day were the arbiters of Italy. After them came all the other captains who down to our own times have commanded the arms of Italy — and the sum of all their virtù is that Italy has been overrun by Charles, plundered by Louis, violated by Ferdinand, and insulted by the Swiss. Their method was this: first, to raise their own standing, they destroyed the standing of the infantry. They did it because, having no state of their own and living off their trade, a few foot soldiers gave them no reputation and many were more than they could feed; so they kept to cavalry, where a manageable number could be both fed and honored. Matters came to the point where in an army of twenty thousand soldiers you would not find two thousand foot. Beyond this, they had used every device to spare themselves and their soldiers hardship and fear: in the skirmishes they did not kill one another, but took prisoners and freed them without ransom; they made no assault on towns by night, and the men in the towns made none on the camps; they built neither stockade nor ditch around their quarters; they did not campaign in winter. All of this their military code permitted, and all of it, as I have said, they invented to escape hardship and danger — until they had brought Italy to slavery and contempt.
books.title: The Kinds of Troops, and Mercenaries

books.label: Chapter XIII
paragraphs: Auxiliaries — the other useless kind of arms — are what you have when you call in a powerful outsider to come with his forces to aid you and defend you, as Pope Julius did in recent memory. Having seen in the Ferrara campaign what a sorry showing his mercenaries made, he turned to auxiliaries, and arranged with Ferdinand, King of Spain, to help him with his men and armies. These arms can be useful and good in themselves, but for the man who calls them in they are almost always ruinous: if they lose, you are undone; if they win, you are their prisoner.

Ancient histories are full of such examples, but I will stay with this fresh one of Pope Julius the Second, whose choice could hardly have been less considered: to get Ferrara, he put himself entirely into a foreigner's hands. Only his good fortune brought forth a third outcome, so that he did not reap the fruit of his bad choice. His auxiliaries were routed at Ravenna; then the Swiss rose up and — against every expectation, his own and everyone else's — chased out the victors. So he ended prisoner neither of his enemies, who had fled, nor of his auxiliaries, since the winning had been done by arms other than theirs.
The Florentines, having no arms at all of their own, brought ten thousand Frenchmen to take Pisa; and by that policy they ran more danger than at any other moment of their troubles.

The Emperor of Constantinople, to oppose his neighbors, put ten thousand Turks into Greece; and when the war was over, they would not leave. That was the beginning of Greece's servitude to the infidel.

So: the man who wants to make sure he cannot win should use these arms. They are far more dangerous than mercenaries, because with them the ruin comes ready-made: they are all one body, and all obedient to someone other than you. Mercenaries, even once they have won, need more time and a better opening to hurt you: they are not one body, and you raised them and you pay them; the outsider you set at their head cannot at once take enough authority to do you damage. In short — with mercenaries the deadliest thing is their cowardice; with auxiliaries, their virtù. Wise princes have therefore always shunned these arms and turned to their own, and have preferred to lose with their own men rather than win with another's, judging no victory real that is won with borrowed arms.

I will never hesitate to cite Cesare Borgia and his actions. This duke entered the Romagna with auxiliary arms, bringing in nothing but French soldiers, and with them he took Imola and Forli. When those arms then struck him as unsafe, he turned to mercenaries, judging the danger there smaller, and hired the Orsini and the Vitelli. Finding these, in the handling, doubtful, disloyal, and dangerous, he destroyed them, and turned to his own men. And the difference between these kinds of arms is easily seen by considering the difference in the duke's reputation when he had the French, when he had the Orsini and Vitelli, and when he stood on his own soldiers and on himself. His reputation grew at every step; and he was never rated so high as when everyone saw that he was complete master of his own forces.

I meant not to go beyond Italian and recent examples, but I am unwilling to leave out Hiero the Syracusan, since he is one of those I named above. Made head of the army by the Syracusans, as I said, he saw at once that mercenary soldiery was useless — its captains were built just like our Italian condottieri. And concluding that he could neither keep them nor let them go, he had them all cut to pieces; after which he made war with his own arms, and not with anyone else's.

I want to recall, too, a figure from the Old Testament made for this subject. When David offered himself to Saul to go and fight Goliath, the Philistine champion, Saul, to give him heart, dressed him in his own armor — and David, once he had it on, refused it, saying he could not give a true account of himself in it: he would meet the enemy with his sling and his knife. In the end, the armor of others falls off your back, or weighs you down, or binds you tight.

Charles the Seventh, father of King Louis the Eleventh, having freed France from the English by his fortune and his virtù, understood this necessity of arming himself with his own arms, and set up in his kingdom the ordinances of the men-at-arms and the infantry. Then his son King Louis abolished the infantry and began to hire the Swiss — a mistake which, followed by others, is now plainly seen to be the source of that kingdom's dangers. For by raising the reputation of the Swiss, he degraded all his own arms: the infantry he wiped out altogether, and his men-at-arms he made dependent on the arms of others, since, being accustomed to fight alongside the Swiss, they no longer believe they can win without them. Hence the French are not enough against the Swiss, and without the Swiss they do not attempt much against anyone else. The armies of France, then, have been mixed — part mercenary, part her own; arms which, taken together, are much better than pure auxiliaries or pure mercenaries, and much inferior to one's own. The example already given is enough: the kingdom of France would be unbeatable today if the ordinance of Charles had been enlarged, or even kept.

But the small wisdom of men will begin a thing that tastes good at the time and never notice the poison underneath — as I said earlier about wasting fevers. The ruler of a principality who does not recognize evils at their birth is not truly wise; and that is given to few. And if you look for the first cause of the ruin of the Roman Empire, you will find it was nothing but the hiring of the Goths: from that beginning the strength of the Roman Empire started to slacken, and all the virtù that drained out of it was handed to them.

I conclude, then, that no principality is secure without arms of its own; it is instead wholly dependent on fortune, having no virtù to defend it faithfully in adversity. And it was ever the opinion and verdict of wise men that nothing is so weak or so unstable as a reputation for power that does not rest on strength of one's own. And one's own arms are those composed of subjects, or of citizens, or of dependents of yours: all others are mercenary or auxiliary. The way to organize your own arms is easily found if you go back over the arrangements of the four men I have named, and if you see how Philip, father of Alexander the Great, and how many republics and princes have armed and ordered themselves. To their methods I defer entirely.
books.title: Auxiliaries, Mixed Troops, and One's Own

books.label: Chapter XIV
paragraphs: A prince, then, should have no other object, no other thought, and take nothing else for his craft, but war, its rules, and its discipline; for that is the only art expected of the man who commands. And it is an art of such virtù that it not only keeps in place those who were born princes, but many times lifts men from private station to that rank — while the reverse is also on record: princes who thought more of luxury than of arms have lost their states. The first thing that loses you your state is neglect of this art; the thing that wins you a state is mastery of it. Francesco Sforza, because he was armed, rose from private citizen to Duke of Milan; his sons, because they fled the hardships of arms, sank from dukes to private citizens. For among the other evils that being unarmed brings you, it makes you despised — one of those disgraces, as will be said below, that a prince must guard against. Between an armed man and an unarmed man there is no proportion at all; and it is not reasonable that the armed should obey the unarmed willingly, or that the unarmed should be safe among armed servants. With disdain on one side and suspicion on the other, they cannot work well together. So a prince who understands nothing of war, beyond the other miseries already mentioned, cannot be respected by his soldiers, and cannot trust them. He should never, therefore, lift his thoughts from the exercise of war; and he should exercise it harder in peace than in war. He can do this in two ways: with action, and with the mind.

As for action: besides keeping his men well ordered and well drilled, he should live in the hunt, hardening his body to exertion and learning the nature of ground as he goes — how the mountains rise, how the valleys open, how the plains lie; what the rivers and marshes are like — and in this he should take the greatest care. The knowledge pays twice. First, he learns to know his own country, and can better see how to defend it. Second, by knowing that terrain and having it under his feet, he grasps with ease any new terrain he must scout; for the hills, valleys, plains, rivers, and marshes of Tuscany, say, bear a certain resemblance to those of other provinces, so that from knowing the ground of one province you come easily to know the ground of others. And the prince who lacks this skill lacks the first quality a captain must have; for it is what teaches you to find your enemy, choose your quarters, lead armies, order a battle, and lay siege to towns with the advantage on your side.

Philopoemen, prince of the Achaeans, among the praises writers have given him, is praised for this: that in peacetime he never thought about anything but the ways of war. When he was in the country with friends, he would often stop and reason with them: "If the enemy were on that hill and we stood here with our army, which of us would have the advantage? How could we go at them, keeping formation? If we wanted to retreat, how would we manage it? If they retreated, how should we pursue?" And as he went he would set before them every chance that can befall an army; he heard their opinions, gave his own, and backed it with reasons — so that, through this endless rehearsal, no accident could ever arise, with his armies in the field, for which he did not have the remedy.

As for exercising the mind, the prince should read histories, and study in them the actions of excellent men: see how they carried themselves in war; examine the causes of their victories and their defeats, so as to flee the one and imitate the other; and above all, do as some excellent man before him has done — take as his model some earlier man who was praised and glorified, and keep that man's deeds and actions always by him, as Alexander the Great is said to have imitated Achilles; Caesar, Alexander; Scipio, Cyrus. And whoever reads the life of Cyrus written by Xenophon will then recognize, in the life of Scipio, how much glory that imitation earned him, and how closely, in chastity, affability, humanity, and generosity, Scipio kept to what Xenophon wrote of Cyrus. Such are the ways a wise prince must observe; and he should never stand idle in peaceful times, but work in them industriously to build up capital he can draw on in adversity — so that when fortune turns, she finds him ready to resist her.
books.title: The Prince and the Art of War

books.label: Chapter XV
paragraphs: It remains now to see what the conduct and bearing of a prince ought to be toward his subjects and his friends. And because I know that many have written on this, I fear that in writing on it too I will be thought presumptuous — the more so because in treating the matter I depart from the paths laid down by others. But since my intention is to write something useful to whoever understands it, it has seemed to me more fitting to go straight after the effectual truth of the thing than after the imagination of it. Many have imagined republics and principalities that no one has ever seen or known to exist in the world as it is; for the way men live is so far from the way men ought to live that whoever lets go of what is done for what ought to be done learns his ruin sooner than his preservation. A man who insists on being good in everything must come to ruin among so many who are not good.

So it is necessary for a prince who wants to keep his state to learn how not to be good, and to use that knowledge, or not use it, as necessity requires. Setting aside, then, the things imagined about a prince, and speaking of the things that are true, I say that all men, whenever they are spoken of — and princes most of all, being set so high — are marked with some one of those qualities that draw blame or praise. One is held generous, another a miser — I use the Tuscan word, since in our tongue an avaricious man is still one who craves to get by plunder, while we call a miser the man who holds back too hard from using what is his own; one is a giver, another grasping; one cruel, another merciful; one a breaker of faith, another a keeper of it; one effeminate and cowardly, another fierce and full of spirit; one humane, another haughty; one lecherous, another chaste; one straightforward, another sly; one hard, another easygoing; one grave, another frivolous; one religious, another unbelieving; and so on. And I know that everyone will admit it would be a most praiseworthy thing for a prince to possess, of all the qualities named above, the ones held to be good. But since they cannot all be had, nor all wholly practiced — the conditions of human life do not allow it — a prince must be prudent enough to know how to escape the infamy of those vices that would take his state from him, and to guard, if he can, against the vices that would not; and if he cannot, he may let those go with less concern. And further, he must not care about incurring infamy for vices without which the state can hardly be saved; because, when everything is weighed, he will find some things that look like virtue and would be his ruin if he followed them, and others that look like vice and bring him, if he follows them, his security and his well-being.
books.title: What Princes Are Praised or Blamed For

books.label: Chapter XXI
paragraphs: Nothing makes a prince so esteemed as great enterprises and rare displays of his own quality. Our own age has Ferdinand of Aragon, the present King of Spain. He can almost be called a new prince, because from a weak king he has become, by fame and glory, the first king in Christendom; and if you examine his deeds you will find them all great, and some of them extraordinary. At the start of his reign he attacked Granada, and that campaign was the foundation of his state. He began it at his leisure and with no fear of interference, for it kept the minds of the barons of Castile fixed on the war and away from any thought of change at home; and meanwhile, without their noticing, he was gaining standing and authority over them. He fed his armies on the money of the Church and of the people, and that long war let him lay a foundation for his own soldiery, which has since brought him honor. Beyond this, always using religion as the pretext for greater designs, he turned to a pious cruelty, hunting the Moors down and clearing them out of his kingdom — no example could be more wretched, or more rare. Under the same cloak he attacked Africa; he made his descent on Italy; he has lately attacked France. So he has never stopped weaving great designs, and they have kept his subjects in suspense and wonder, absorbed in waiting to see how things would come out. And each of his moves has been born out of the last, so that between one and the next, men have never had a quiet stretch in which to work against him.

It also helps a prince a great deal to give rare examples of himself in domestic affairs, like those told of Messer Bernabo da Milano: whenever anyone in civic life did something extraordinary, good or bad, he seized the occasion to reward or punish him in a way that people would talk about for a long time. And above all, a prince must strive in everything he does to earn the name of a great man of exceptional intelligence.

A prince is also esteemed when he is a true friend and a true enemy — when, without hedging, he comes out openly for one side against another. That course is always more useful than standing neutral. For if two of your powerful neighbors come to blows, either the winner will be a threat to you afterward or he will not. In either case it will always be better for you to declare yourself and wage war in earnest. In the first case, if you do not declare yourself, you will be the prize of whoever wins — to the pleasure and satisfaction of whoever loses — and you will have no defense to offer and no reason anyone should give you one, and no one will take you in. The winner does not want doubtful friends who would not stand by him in hard times; the loser will not shelter you, because you would not take up your sword and run his fortune with him.

Antiochus came into Greece, brought in by the Ætolians to drive out the Romans. He sent envoys to the Achaeans, who were friends of the Romans, urging them to stay neutral; the Romans, meanwhile, were urging them to take up arms for their side. The question came before the council of the Achaeans, and when the legate of Antiochus pressed them toward neutrality, the Roman legate answered: “As for the course these men praise as best and most useful for your state — that you keep out of our war — nothing is further from your interest: keep out, and without thanks and without dignity you will be the winner's prize.” So it will always go: the one who is not your friend will ask you for neutrality, and the one who is your friend will ask you to declare yourself with arms. Irresolute princes, trying to escape the danger of the moment, take the neutral road most of the time, and most of the time they are ruined. But when a prince declares himself boldly for one side, then if his ally wins — however powerful the winner, however much you lie at his mercy — he is in your debt; a bond of affection has been formed; and men are never so shameless as to crush you with so flagrant a show of ingratitude. Besides, victories are never so clean that the winner can throw off every restraint, least of all justice. And if your ally loses, he takes you in; while he can, he helps you; and you become companions of a fortune that can rise again.

In the second case, when the two who fight are such that you have nothing to fear from whichever of them wins, it is all the more prudent to take a side: you help destroy the one with the aid of the other, who ought to have rescued him if he had been wise; and since with your help he cannot fail to win, he wins and remains at your discretion. And here it should be noted that a prince ought never to make common cause with someone more powerful than himself in order to attack others, unless necessity forces him, as was said above: for if your stronger partner wins, you are his prisoner, and princes should do all they can to avoid lying at anyone's discretion. The Venetians allied themselves with France against the Duke of Milan — a ruinous alliance they could have avoided. But when it cannot be avoided, as it could not be for the Florentines when the Pope and Spain marched their armies into Lombardy, then the prince should commit himself, for the reasons given.

And let no state ever believe it can choose a safe course; let it expect instead to choose among doubtful ones. For this is in the order of things: you never escape one trouble without walking into another. Prudence consists in knowing how to weigh the troubles against each other, and to take the least bad as good.

A prince should also show himself a lover of excellence, giving a place to able men and honoring those who are outstanding in any art. Beyond that, he should encourage his citizens to follow their occupations in peace — in trade, in farming, in every other human pursuit — so that no one is afraid to improve his property for fear it will be taken from him, and no one afraid to open a business for fear of the taxman. Instead he should hold out rewards for whoever wants to do these things, and for anyone who thinks of any way at all of enlarging his city or his state.

Beyond this, at the fitting seasons of the year, he should keep the people occupied with festivals and spectacles. And since every city is divided into guilds or wards, he should take account of those bodies, meet with them now and then, and show himself in his own person an example of courtesy and generosity — all the while holding the majesty of his rank firm, for that must never be allowed to slip in anything.
books.title: How a Prince Wins Esteem

books.label: Chapter XXII
paragraphs: The choice of ministers is no small matter for a prince: they are good or not according to the prince's own prudence. The first guess one makes about a ruler's brains comes from seeing the men he keeps around him. When they are capable and faithful, you can always count him wise, because he knew how to recognize their capacity and how to keep them faithful. When they are otherwise, you can always judge him badly, for the first error he made was in this choice.

No one who knew Messer Antonio da Venafro as the minister of Pandolfo Petrucci, prince of Siena, could help judging Pandolfo a most able man for having Venafro as his minister. For there are three kinds of brains: one understands things on its own; the second discerns what others understand; the third understands neither on its own nor through others. The first is most excellent, the second excellent, the third useless. So it necessarily followed that if Pandolfo was not in the first rank, he was in the second: for whenever a man has the judgment to recognize the good and the bad in what another says and does, then even if he has no invention of his own, he can tell his minister's good work from his bad, praise the one and correct the other; and the minister, who cannot hope to fool him, keeps himself good.

But as for how a prince may know his minister, there is a test that never fails. When you see a minister thinking more about himself than about you, and hunting his own profit inside everything he does, a man made that way will never be a good minister, and you will never be able to trust him. For the man who holds another's state in his hands must never think of himself but always of his prince, and must never put before him any business that is not the prince's own.

And on the other side, to keep the minister good, the prince should think of him in turn: honor him, enrich him, bind him with obligations, share the honors and the burdens with him — so that the minister sees he cannot stand without the prince; so that abundant honors leave him wanting no more honors, abundant riches leave him wanting no more riches, and his full load of responsibilities makes him dread any change of regime. When ministers, and princes in their dealings with ministers, are made this way, each can trust the other; and when they are otherwise, it ends badly for one or the other, every time.
books.title: A Prince's Ministers

books.label: Chapter XXIII
paragraphs: I do not want to leave out an important topic, and a mistake princes can hardly defend themselves against unless they are very shrewd, or choose their men very well. I mean the flatterers, and the courts are full of them. For men take such pleasure in their own doings, and deceive themselves about them so thoroughly, that they can barely protect themselves from this plague; and the attempt to protect yourself brings a danger of its own — the danger of becoming despised. There is no way to guard against flattery but to have men understand that telling you the truth does not offend you; yet when everyone may tell you the truth, the reverence goes.

Therefore a prudent prince takes a third way. He chooses wise men from his state, and to them alone he gives free leave to speak the truth to him — and only on the matters he asks about, nothing else. But he should ask them about everything, hear their opinions, and then decide by himself, in his own manner. With these counselors, singly and together, he should carry himself so that every one of them knows the more freely he speaks, the more welcome he will be. Outside of them he should listen to no one, go straight after the thing once decided, and be stubborn in his decisions. Whoever does otherwise is either wrecked by the flatterers, or changes course so often under the pull of contrary opinions that he comes to be despised.

On this point I want to give a modern example. Fra Luca, servant of Maximilian, the present emperor, said of his majesty that he took counsel with no one, and yet never did anything the way he wanted. This came of his doing the opposite of what I have described. For the emperor is a secretive man: he tells no one his plans and takes no advice on them. But as the plans go into effect they begin to show and be discovered, and then the men around him begin to talk him out of them; and he, being pliable, is turned aside. So what he does one day he undoes the next; no one ever understands what he wants or intends to do; and no one can build on his decisions.

A prince, therefore, should always take counsel — but when he wants it, not when others want to give it. In fact he should discourage anyone from volunteering advice on anything unless he asks for it. But he himself should be a generous asker of questions, and then, about the things he asked, a patient hearer of the truth; indeed, when he learns that anyone out of some scruple is keeping the truth from him, he should let his anger show.

Many people suppose that a prince who gives an impression of prudence owes it not to his own nature but to the good advisers around him. They are certainly deceived. For this is a general rule that never fails: a prince who is not wise himself cannot be advised well — unless by chance he hands himself over entirely to a single man of great prudence who governs everything for him. In that case he might indeed be well governed, but it would not last long, because that governor would in short order take the state away from him.

But taking counsel from more than one, a prince who is not wise will never get counsels that agree, and he will not know how to reconcile them himself. Each counselor will think of his own interest; the prince will know neither how to correct them nor how to see through them. And counselors come no other way, because men will always turn out bad for you unless some necessity makes them good. So the conclusion is this: good counsel, wherever it comes from, must be born of the prince's prudence — the prince's prudence is not born of good counsel.
books.title: Avoiding Flatterers

books.label: Chapter XXIV
paragraphs: The measures set out above, prudently observed, make a new prince seem an old one, and settle him faster and more firmly in his state than if he had grown old in it. For a new prince is watched far more closely in his actions than a hereditary one; and when his actions are recognized as able, they take hold of men far more, and bind them far tighter, than ancient blood does. For men are taken much more by present things than by past ones, and when they find the present good they enjoy it and look for nothing else — indeed they will mount every defense of such a prince, so long as he does not fail them in the rest. And so he will have a double glory: to have founded a new principality, and to have adorned and strengthened it with good laws, good arms, good allies, and good examples — just as the man born a prince who loses his state through lack of prudence carries a double shame.

And if you consider the lords who have lost their states in Italy in our times — the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the rest — you will find in them, first, one common defect in the matter of arms, for the causes discussed at length above; and then you will see that some of them either had the people for enemies, or, if they had the people friendly, did not know how to secure the great men. Without these defects, states are not lost that have sinew enough to keep an army in the field.

Philip of Macedon — not Alexander's father, but the one Titus Quintius defeated — did not have much of a state, measured against the greatness of the Romans and of the Greece that attacked him. Yet because he was a military man who knew how to hold the people and secure the great, he sustained the war against them for years; and if in the end he lost his grip on a few cities, the kingdom stayed his.

So let these princes of ours, who held their principalities for years on end and then lost them, blame not fortune but their own laziness. In quiet times they never once considered that things can change — it is the common defect of men not to reckon on the storm while the sea is calm — and when the hard times came, their thoughts ran to flight and not to defense, and they hoped the people, disgusted by the winners' insolence, would call them back. That plan, when all others are gone, is good; but it is very bad to have let the other remedies go for its sake. You should never accept a fall on the faith that someone will be there to pick you up. Either it does not happen, or, if it happens, it brings you no safety — because that kind of rescue is a coward's defense and does not depend on you. The only defenses that are good, that are certain, that are lasting, are the ones that depend on you yourself and on your own strength.
books.title: Why Italy's Princes Lost Their States

books.label: Chapter XXV
paragraphs: I am well aware that many men have held, and hold, the opinion that the affairs of the world are so governed by fortune and by God that human prudence cannot correct them — that there is no remedy at all; and on this account they might judge that there is no point sweating over anything, and that we should let ourselves be governed by chance. This opinion has gained more credit in our times because of the great upheavals in affairs that have been seen, and are seen every day, beyond anything anyone could have guessed. Thinking it over, I have myself leaned some way toward their opinion at times. Nevertheless — so that our free will is not extinguished — I judge it may be true that fortune is arbiter of half of our actions, but that she leaves the other half, or close to it, for us to govern.

I compare her to one of those ruinous rivers that, when they grow angry, flood the plains, tear down trees and buildings, lift the earth from this bank and lay it on that one. Everyone flees before the water; everyone gives way to its fury, powerless to stand against it anywhere. And yet, though rivers are made this way, it does not follow that men in quiet weather cannot prepare — with embankments and dikes — so that when the waters rise again they either run off down a channel, or their rush is neither so wild nor so ruinous. It is the same with fortune. She shows her power where no ordered strength stands ready to resist her, and she turns her floods where she knows no dikes and no embankments have been raised to hold her.

And if you consider Italy — the seat of these upheavals, and the country that set them moving — you will see an open plain without dikes and without a single embankment. Had she been protected by proper strength, as Germany, Spain, and France are, either this flood would never have made the great changes it has made, or it would not have come at all. And let this be enough said about resisting fortune in general.

But narrowing myself to particulars, I say that one sees a prince prosper today and fall tomorrow with no visible change in his nature or in any quality he has. This, I believe, comes first from the causes already discussed at length: the prince who leans entirely on fortune falls the moment she turns. I believe, further, that the man prospers who matches his way of proceeding to the quality of the times, and likewise that the man fails whose proceedings are at odds with the times. For in the things that carry men toward the end each one aims at — glory and riches — you see them proceed differently: one with caution, another with a rush; one by force, the other by craft; one by patience, the other by its opposite; and each can arrive by his own road. You also see two cautious men, one reaching his goal and the other not; and again two men prospering equally by opposite methods, one cautious, the other impetuous. All of this comes from nothing but the quality of the times, which either agrees with a man's way of proceeding or does not. From this follows what I said: that two men working differently produce the same effect, and of two working alike, one arrives and the other does not.

On this also hangs the swing of prosperity. If a man governs himself with caution and patience, and times and affairs revolve in a way that makes his method the right one, he prospers; but if times and affairs change, he is ruined, because he does not change his way of proceeding. And no man is found so prudent that he knows how to fit himself to this — both because he cannot swerve from what his own nature inclines him to, and because, having always prospered by walking one road, he cannot be persuaded to leave it. So the cautious man, when the moment comes to strike out, does not know how to do it, and down he goes; whereas if he could change his nature with the times and with affairs, his fortune would not change.

Pope Julius the Second proceeded impetuously in everything he did, and he found the times and circumstances so agreeable to his way of proceeding that things always came out well for him. Consider his first campaign, against Bologna, while Messer Giovanni Bentivogli still lived. The Venetians did not like it; neither did the King of Spain; with France he still had the enterprise under negotiation — and nonetheless, with his usual ferocity and drive, he led the expedition in person. The move left Spain and the Venetians standing frozen, the latter out of fear, the former out of appetite to recover the whole Kingdom of Naples; and at the same time it dragged the King of France in behind him, for the king, seeing him already in motion and wanting the Pope as a friend against the Venetians, judged he could not refuse him troops without an open insult. So with one impetuous stroke Julius accomplished what no other pontiff, with all human prudence, would ever have accomplished. Had he waited in Rome until his plans were settled and everything arranged, as any other pontiff would have done, he would never have succeeded: the King of France would have found a thousand excuses, and the others would have raised a thousand fears.

I will pass over his other deeds, which were all of a piece, and all of them turned out well; and the shortness of his life never let him taste the contrary. For if times had come that required him to proceed with caution, his ruin would have followed: he would never have swerved from the ways his nature inclined him to.

I conclude, then, that since fortune changes and men stand stubborn in their ways, they prosper so long as the two run together, and fail the moment they part. For my own part I judge this: it is better to be impetuous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you mean to keep her down you must beat her and shove her. And plainly she lets herself be won by such men sooner than by those who proceed coldly. And so, like a woman, she is always the friend of the young — because they are less cautious, fiercer, and command her with more audacity.
books.title: Fortune, and How to Resist Her

books.label: Chapter XXVI
paragraphs: Having considered everything discussed above, I have been asking myself whether in Italy, right now, the times are ripe to honor a new prince — whether the material lies here that would give a prudent and able man the occasion to shape it into a form that would bring honor to him and good to the whole body of her people. And it seems to me that so many things now run together in a new prince's favor that I do not know what time was ever more fit for one.

If, as I said, the people of Israel had to be slaves in Egypt for the power in Moses to show itself; if the Persians had to be crushed by the Medes for the greatness of Cyrus's spirit to be known, and the Athenians scattered for the excellence of Theseus to appear — then now, for the worth of one Italian spirit to be known, Italy had to be brought down to her present extremity: more enslaved than the Hebrews, more servile than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians; without a head, without order; beaten, stripped, torn, overrun; made to endure ruin of every kind.

And though before now a glimmer showed in one man, enough to let us think God had ordained him for her redemption, still we saw how afterward, at the very height of his course, fortune cast him off. So she lies there as if lifeless, waiting for whoever it may be that can heal her wounds — put an end to the sacking of Lombardy, to the extortion of the kingdom and of Tuscany — and clean out the sores that have festered now for so long. See how she prays God to send someone to redeem her from these cruelties and this barbarian insolence. See how ready she is, how willing, to march behind a flag — if only someone would raise one.

Nor is there anyone now in view in whom she can place more hope than in your illustrious house, which — with its fortune and its ability, favored by God and by the Church, of which it is now the head — can make itself the leader of this redemption. That will not be very hard if you hold before your eyes the deeds and the lives of the men named above. They were rare and marvelous men; but they were men, and none of them had an opportunity as good as this one: their enterprise was not more just than this, nor easier, nor was God more a friend to them than he is to you.

Here justice is great: for war is just for those to whom it is necessary, and arms are holy where there is no hope left except in arms. Here the willingness is very great; and where the willingness is great, the difficulty cannot be great, provided your house takes as its mark the methods of the men I have held up. Beyond this, extraordinary things without precedent have been seen here, God leading the way: the sea has opened; a cloud has shown the road; the rock has poured out water; manna has rained down. Everything has run together toward your greatness. The rest you must do yourselves. God does not want to do everything, lest he take from us our free will and the share of the glory that falls to us.

And it is no wonder if none of the Italians named before could do what we may hope from your illustrious house, or if in so many revolutions and so many campaigns of war in Italy it always looks as if military virtue were spent. The truth is that her old institutions were bad, and no one has appeared who knew how to find new ones. Nothing brings a newly risen man so much honor as the new laws and new institutions he devises: when they are well founded and have greatness in them, they make him revered and admired. And in Italy the material is not lacking — it will take any form you can give it.

Here there is great strength in the limbs, if only it were not missing in the heads. Look at the duels and the small combats: how superior the Italians are in strength, in dexterity, in quickness of wit. But when it comes to armies they make no showing. And all of it traces back to the weakness of the heads: the men who know are not obeyed, every man thinks he knows, and no one until now has known how to lift himself, by ability or by fortune, so far above the rest that the others would yield to him. That is why, over so long a time, through so many wars in the past twenty years, whenever an army has been all Italian it has always failed the test. The first witness is Il Taro; then Allesandria, Capua, Genoa, Vaila, Bologna, Mestri.

If your illustrious house, then, means to follow those excellent men who redeemed their countries, one thing is necessary before all others, the true foundation of every such enterprise: to arm yourself with your own troops, for there can be no more faithful, truer, or better soldiers. And good as each man of them is singly, together they will be better still when they see themselves commanded by their own prince, honored by him, and kept at his charge. These arms must be prepared, so that with Italian strength we can defend ourselves against the foreigner.

The Swiss and the Spanish infantry are counted terrifying, it is true; yet each has a defect, so that a third order of troops could not only stand against them but be confident of beating them. For the Spaniards cannot withstand cavalry, and the Swiss have reason to fear infantry that meets them in close combat as stubbornly as they fight. So we have seen, and will see again by experience, that the Spaniards cannot hold against French cavalry, and the Swiss are broken by Spanish infantry. Of this last there is no complete proof yet, but a taste of it was given at the battle of Ravenna, when the Spanish infantry met the German battalions, which keep the same order as the Swiss: the Spaniards, with the agility of their bodies and the help of their bucklers, got in under the Germans' pikes and stood there safe, cutting at them while the Germans had no remedy; and had the cavalry not charged them, the Spaniards would have finished them all. Knowing the defect of both these infantries, then, one can order a new kind, able to stand against horse and unafraid of foot — and this will be done by the kind of arms chosen and a change of formations. These are among the things which, ordered fresh, give reputation and greatness to a new prince.

This opportunity, then, must not be let slip, so that Italy, after so long, may at last see her redeemer. I cannot express with what love he would be received in all the provinces that have suffered these foreign floods; with what thirst for vengeance, what stubborn faith, what devotion, what tears. What doors would be shut against him? What people would refuse him obedience? What envy would set itself against him? What Italian would withhold his homage? To every one of us this barbarian rule stinks. Let your illustrious house take up this cause, then, with the spirit and the hope in which just enterprises are taken up; so that under its banner this country may be made noble again, and under its auspices Petrarch's words may come true:

Virtù contro al Furore
prenderà l'arme, e fia il combatter corto:
ché l'antico valore
negli italici cuor non è ancor morto.

Virtue against fury
will take up arms; and the fight will be short:
for the ancient valor
in Italian hearts is not yet dead.
